title: Plurals of Paucity, Multitude & Plural of Plurals
source: Original instructional lesson authored for this application (syllabus ref: Haywood & Nahmad Ch. 43; Ryding Ch. 6–7)
objectives: Recognize the four patterns of plurals of paucity (jamʿ al-qillah, denoting 3–10): أَفْعُلٌ, أَفْعَالٌ, أَفْعِلَةٌ, فِعْلَةٌ.
Distinguish plurals of paucity from plurals of multitude (jamʿ al-kathrah).
Recognize plural of plurals (jamʿ al-jamʿ) in classical prose.
recallPrompt: From Chapter 36: Which number band (3–10 or 11–99) takes a plural genitive counted noun?

sections.heading: Paucity (3–10) vs. Multitude (11+)
sections.body: Some Arabic nouns possess two broken plurals: a plural of paucity (jamʿ al-qillah) used classically for small counts (3–10), and a plural of multitude (jamʿ al-kathrah) for larger numbers. Classical texts also occasionally form a 'plural of a plural' (jamʿ al-jamʿ) to express great abundance.

sections.label: The Four Plurals of Paucity
sections.summary: Only four broken plural patterns belong to jamʿ al-qillah: أَفْعُلٌ (أَشْهُرٌ 'months'), أَفْعَالٌ (أَيَّامٌ 'days'), أَفْعِلَةٌ (أَسْئِلَةٌ 'questions'), and فِعْلَةٌ (فِتْيَةٌ 'youths').

sections.irab: ثَلَاثَةُ: مُضَافٌ مَرْفُوعٌ | أَشْهُرٍ: مُضَافٌ إِلَيْهِ مَجْرُورٌ (جَمْعُ قِلَّةٍ)
sections.notes: For counts 3–10, classical style prefers the plural of paucity أَشْهُرٍ over شُهُورٍ.

sections.heading: Most Nouns Have Only One Plural
sections.body: When a noun has only a single broken plural, that one form is used for all counts (both 3–10 and general plurality).
